task.prompt: A planar 2R arm uses relative joint angles q1 = 3π/4 rad and q2 = -π/2 rad (counter-clockwise positive, q1 measured from the +x axis). What is the tool orientation, the world angle of link 2, modulo 2π?
task.solution: Tool orientation = q1 + q2 = 3π/4 + (-π/2) = π/4 rad. -π/2 rad is q2 alone (treating q2 as a world angle), 3π/4 rad is q1 alone (ignoring the elbow), and -3π/4 rad comes from q1 - q2.
hints: With relative joints, link 2 is turned by q2 from the direction of link 1, which itself points at q1.
Add the two joint angles: 3π/4 + (-π/2). Write both with a denominator of 4 before adding, then reduce modulo 2π if needed.

task.remediation: If you chose -π/2 rad, you read q2 as an absolute angle; relative joint angles add along the chain. Revisit the relative-angle convention in /lessons/R04, then practise a fresh X11 item before another independent check.

task.prompt: A planar 2R arm has l1 = 1.8 m and l2 = 0.7 m, with relative joint angles q1 = 0.9 rad and q2 = π rad. What is the straight-line distance from the base to the tip? Give 3 decimal places; tolerance ±0.001 m.
task.solution: r² = l1² + l2² + 2 l1 l2 cos π = (l1 - l2)², so r = |l1 - l2| = |1.8 - 0.7| = 1.1 m. q1 = 0.9 rad only rotates the folded arm about the base and does not change r. A distance is never negative.
hints: q2 = π turns link 2 back by half a turn relative to link 1. Ask which joint angle the base-to-tip distance actually depends on.
The distance satisfies r² = l1² + l2² + 2 l1 l2 cos q2, which does not contain q1. Substitute cos π = -1 and simplify before taking the square root.

task.prompt: A planar 2R arm uses relative joint angles. Only q2 changes; q1, l1 and l2 stay fixed. Which quantity is guaranteed to stay the same?
task.solution: The elbow is at (l1 cos q1, l1 sin q1), which contains only q1 and l1, so it stays fixed. The tip, the tool orientation q1 + q2 and the base-to-tip distance sqrt(l1² + l2² + 2 l1 l2 cos q2) all change with q2.
hints: Picture the arm and decide which links move when joint 2 turns: a joint moves everything after it in the chain.

task.prompt: Your planar 2R forward-kinematics calculation for given l1, l2, q1, q2 is exactly right. What does that result establish?

fields.label: Conclusion
fields.answer: the tip pose of the ideal planar model at those joint angles
options: the joint angles needed to reach any chosen tip point
the tip pose of the ideal planar model at those joint angles

task.solution: A correct FK result establishes only the tip pose of the ideal planar model at the given joint angles. Reaching a chosen point is inverse kinematics, a 3D arm needs a spatial model, and real-robot accuracy needs calibration and measurement.
hints: Forward kinematics maps given joint angles to a pose of an ideal model. Ask which option is exactly that map and nothing more.

task.prompt: A planar 2R forward-kinematics routine returns the correct x, y and theta for every tested set of joint angles. Which conclusion is justified by that alone?

fields.label: Conclusion
fields.answer: it computes the ideal-model tool pose for given joint angles
options: it can choose joint angles that reach a requested tip point
the real arm may be commanded without further hardware checks
it computes the ideal-model tool pose for given joint angles
it describes a 6-joint spatial arm once two angles are fixed

task.solution: Passing FK tests shows the routine computes the ideal-model pose for given joint angles. Choosing angles for a target is inverse kinematics, a 6-joint spatial arm is outside the planar model, and commanding hardware needs separate safety and accuracy checks.
hints: Forward kinematics maps given joint angles to a pose of an ideal model. Ask which option is exactly that map and nothing more.
Inverse kinematics runs the map backwards, spatial arms need a 3D model, and physical accuracy depends on calibration, backlash and sensing, none of which a planar formula contains.

Passing FK tests shows the routine computes the ideal-model pose for given joint angles. Choosing angles for a target is inverse kinematics, a 6-joint spatial arm is outside the planar model, and commanding hardware needs separate safety and accuracy checks.
task.remediation: Treat a correct FK pose as a claim about the ideal planar model only; inverse kinematics, spatial chains and hardware accuracy are separate claims. Re-read what the R04 objective excludes (inverse kinematics, spatial chains, physical accuracy) in /lessons/R04 before another independent check.

task.prompt: A planar 2R arm has l1 = l2 = 1.1 m. Configuration A has relative joint angles (q1, q2) = (0.2, 1.0) rad and configuration B has (1.2, -1) rad. Both place the tip at the same point. What are the tool orientations (world angle of link 2) of A and B, in that order?
task.solution: theta_A = 0.2 + 1.0 = 1.2 rad and theta_B = 1.2 + (-1) = 0.2 rad. The tips coincide (elbow-up and elbow-down solutions), but the tool orientations differ, so a pose is more than a tip position. 0.7 rad is the direction of the tip seen from the base, not a link orientation.
hints: Reaching the same tip point does not fix the direction of link 2; compute each configuration's orientation from its own joint angles.
For A add 0.2 + 1.0; for B add 1.2 + (-1).

task.remediation: If you chose a single orientation for both, you assumed that equal tip positions imply equal poses; orientation is a separate output of FK. Revisit the paragraph on one endpoint reached by different configurations in /lessons/R04, then practise a fresh X11 item before another independent check.

task.prompt: Planar 2R arm: l1 = 1.6 m, l2 = 1.3 m; relative joint angles q1 = -0.7 rad, q2 = 1.2 rad (counter-clockwise positive; base at the origin, q1 measured from the +x axis). Compute the tip position x, y and the tool orientation theta (the world angle of link 2) modulo 2π. Give 3 decimal places; tolerance ±0.001 m for x, y and ±0.001 rad for theta.
task.solution: Elbow: (l1 cos q1, l1 sin q1) = (1.6 cos -0.7, 1.6 sin -0.7) = (1.2237475, -1.0307483) m. Link 2 points at the world angle q1 + q2 = -0.7 + 1.2 = 0.5 rad, so it adds (l2 cos(q1 + q2), l2 sin(q1 + q2)) = (1.1408573, 0.6232532) m. Tip: x = 1.2237475 + 1.1408573 = 2.3646048 m; y = -1.0307483 + 0.6232532 = -0.4074951 m. theta = q1 + q2 = 0.5 rad (any value that differs by a multiple of 2π is also accepted).
hints: Relative joints: link 1 points at q1 = -0.7 rad from the +x axis, and link 2 points at the world angle q1 + q2, not at q2 = 1.2 rad alone. Keep the calculator in radian mode.
Elbow first: (1.6 cos -0.7, 1.6 sin -0.7) = (1.2237475, -1.0307483) m. Next add a vector of length l2 = 1.3 m pointing at the world angle q1 + q2 = 0.5 rad.

Elbow: (l1 cos q1, l1 sin q1) = (1.6 cos -0.7, 1.6 sin -0.7) = (1.2237475, -1.0307483) m. Link 2 points at the world angle q1 + q2 = -0.7 + 1.2 = 0.5 rad, so it adds (l2 cos(q1 + q2), l2 sin(q1 + q2)) = (1.1408573, 0.6232532) m. Tip: x = 1.2237475 + 1.1408573 = 2.3646048 m; y = -1.0307483 + 0.6232532 = -0.4074951 m. theta = q1 + q2 = 0.5 rad (any value that differs by a multiple of 2π is also accepted).
task.remediation: Common slips on this item: treating q2 = 1.2 rad as the world angle of link 2 gives x ≈ 1.6948, y ≈ 0.1809 and theta = 1.2; a calculator in degree mode gives x ≈ 2.8998, y ≈ -0.0082. If your answer matches one of these, the slip is in the angle convention, not the formula. Revisit the relative-angle convention in /lessons/R04, then practise a fresh X11 item before another independent check.

task.prompt: Planar 2R arm: l1 = 1.3 m, l2 = 0.6 m; relative joint angles q1 = -2.4 rad, q2 = -1.2 rad (counter-clockwise positive; base at the origin, q1 measured from the +x axis). Compute the tip position x, y and the tool orientation theta (the world angle of link 2) modulo 2π. Give 3 decimal places; tolerance ±0.001 m for x, y and ±0.001 rad for theta. You may leave theta unwrapped; if you reduce it, use 2π ≈ 6.2832.
task.solution: Elbow: (l1 cos q1, l1 sin q1) = (1.3 cos -2.4, 1.3 sin -2.4) = (-0.9586, -0.8781) m. Link 2 points at the world angle q1 + q2 = -2.4 + (-1.2) = -3.6 rad, so it adds (l2 cos(q1 + q2), l2 sin(q1 + q2)) = (-0.5381, 0.2655) m. Tip: x = -0.9586 + (-0.5381) = -1.4967 m; y = -0.8781 + 0.2655 = -0.6126 m. theta = q1 + q2 = -3.6 rad, which lies outside (-π, π]; adding 2π gives -3.6 + 6.2832 = 2.6832 rad. Both -3.6 and 2.6832 are accepted, because orientation is compared modulo 2π.
